outline: 1942 Permutations involving Grouping, Complements, and Cases

examples.question_text: A committee of $3$ is chosen uniformly at random from $6$ teachers and $5$ parents. Find the probability that all committee members are teachers.
examples.solution_text:
Order does not matter, so count committees using combinations.
Total committees: $\binom{11}{3}=165$.
All-teacher committees: $\binom{6}{3}=20$.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{all teachers})&=\frac{20}{165}\\&=\frac{4}{33}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A bag contains $5$ red and $7$ blue counters. Four counters are selected uniformly at random without replacement. Find the probability of selecting exactly $2$ red counters.
examples.solution_text:
Choose $2$ red counters and $2$ blue counters.
Total selections: $\binom{12}{4}=495$.
Favourable selections: $\binom{5}{2}\binom{7}{2}=210$.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{exactly two red})&=\frac{210}{495}\\&=\frac{14}{33}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A committee of $5$ is selected uniformly at random from $7$ musicians and $5$ actors. Find the probability that musicians form a majority.
examples.solution_text:
Total committees: $\binom{12}{5}=792$.
A musician majority means $3$, $4$ or $5$ musicians. These cases do not overlap.
Three musicians: $\binom{7}{3}\binom{5}{2}=350$.
Four musicians: $\binom{7}{4}\binom{5}{1}=175$.
Five musicians: $\binom{7}{5}\binom{5}{0}=21$.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{musician majority})&=\frac{350+175+21}{792}\\&=\frac{91}{132}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A box contains $8$ working batteries and $4$ faulty batteries. Three batteries are selected uniformly at random without replacement. Find the probability that at least one is faulty.
examples.solution_text:
The complement is selecting three working batteries.
Total selections: $\binom{12}{3}=220$.
Selections with no faulty batteries: $\binom{8}{3}=56$.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least one faulty})&=1-\frac{56}{220}\\&=\frac{41}{55}\end{aligned}$

Total arrangements: $7!$.
(a) Treat Ava and Ben as one unit. Arrange the six units, then arrange the pair within their unit.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{together})&=\frac{6!\times2!}{7!}\\&=\frac{2}{7}\end{aligned}$
(b) Use the complement.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{not together})&=1-\frac{2}{7}\\&=\frac{5}{7}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Nine distinct books—$2$ history books, $3$ science books and $4$ novels—are arranged in a uniformly random order on a shelf. Find the probability that each category forms one consecutive block.
examples.solution_text:
Total arrangements: $9!$.
Treat each category as one unit. Arrange the three units, then arrange the books within each unit.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{category blocks})&=\frac{3!\times2!\times3!\times4!}{9!}\\&=\frac{1}{210}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Five boys and five girls sit in a uniformly random order in a row of ten chairs. Find the probability that boys and girls alternate.
examples.solution_text:
Total arrangements: $10!$.
The two possible patterns are BGBGBGBGBG and GBGBGBGBGB. Each allows $5!$ arrangements of the boys and $5!$ arrangements of the girls.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{alternate})&=\frac{2\times5!\times5!}{10!}\\&=\frac{1}{126}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Eight friends sit uniformly at random around a circular table. Find the probability that three particular friends occupy three consecutive seats. Rotations count as the same arrangement.
examples.solution_text:
Total circular arrangements: $(8-1)!=7!$.
Treat the three friends as one unit with the five others. Arrange these six units around the circle, then arrange the three friends within their unit.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{three together})&=\frac{(6-1)!\times3!}{7!}\\&=\frac{1}{7}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Ten people, including Noor and Eli, sit uniformly at random around a circular table with equally spaced seats. Find the probability that Eli sits directly opposite Noor.
A three-digit number is selected uniformly at random from those formed using $3$ different digits from $\{2,3,4,5,6,7\}$. Find the probability that it is even.
examples.solution_text:
Total numbers: ${}^{6}P_3=120$.
Choose the restricted position first: the units digit is $2$, $4$ or $6$. Then fill the first two positions from the five remaining digits.
Favourable numbers: $3\times{}^{5}P_2=60$.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{even})&=\frac{60}{120}\\&=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A three-digit number is selected uniformly at random from those formed using $3$ different digits from $\{2,3,4,5,6\}$. Find the probability that it is divisible by $3$.
examples.solution_text:
Total numbers: ${}^{5}P_3=60$.
The digit sum must be divisible by $3$. The valid sets are $\{2,3,4\}$, $\{2,4,6\}$, $\{3,4,5\}$ and $\{4,5,6\}$.
Each set gives $3!$ arrangements, so there are $4\times3!=24$ favourable numbers.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{divisible by three})&=\frac{24}{60}\\&=\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: The letters of PLANETS are arranged uniformly at random in a row. Find the probability that P and S are separated by at least three letters.
examples.solution_text:
Total arrangements: $7!$.
Subtract the cases with zero, one or two letters between P and S. Their order can be reversed in $2!$ ways.
No letters between: $6!\times2!$.
One letter between: $5\times5!\times2!$.
Two letters between: ${}^{5}P_2\times4!\times2!$.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least three between})&=1-\frac{6!\times2!+5\times5!\times2!+{}^{5}P_2\times4!\times2!}{7!}\\&=1-\frac{3600}{5040}\\&=\frac{2}{7}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Three cards are selected uniformly at random without replacement from a standard deck of $52$ cards. Find the probability that all three have different suits.
examples.solution_text:
Total hands: $\binom{52}{3}=22100$.
Choose three of the four suits, then one of the thirteen cards from each chosen suit.
Favourable hands: $\binom{4}{3}\binom{13}{1}^{3}=8788$.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{different suits})&=\frac{8788}{22100}\\&=\frac{169}{425}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Six cards are selected uniformly at random without replacement from a standard deck of $52$ cards. Find the probability that all six have the same suit.
examples.solution_text:
Total hands: $\binom{52}{6}=20358520$.
Choose the suit, then select six cards from its thirteen cards. The four suit cases do not overlap.
Favourable hands: $\binom{4}{1}\binom{13}{6}=6864$.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{same suit})&=\frac{6864}{20358520}\\&=\frac{66}{195755}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Five cards are selected uniformly at random from a deck containing the four suits of each rank from $2$ to $10$ ($36$ cards in total). Find the probability of a full house: three cards of one rank and two cards of another rank.
examples.solution_text:
Total hands: $\binom{36}{5}=376992$.
Choose the triple's rank from nine ranks and three of its four cards. Choose the pair's rank from the eight remaining ranks and two of its four cards.
Favourable hands: $\binom{9}{1}\binom{4}{3}\binom{8}{1}\binom{4}{2}=1728$.
The triple and pair have different roles, so no division by $2$ is needed.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{full house})&=\frac{1728}{376992}\\&=\frac{6}{1309}\end{aligned}$

coverage.summary: Repaired only example 14's final fraction, replacing 18/3927 with 6/1309. Independently confirmed its booklet-aligned full-house method: 9 × 4 × 8 × 6 = 1728 favourable hands, binomial(36,5) = 376992 total hands, and their greatest common divisor is 288, giving 6/1309 in lowest terms. Its relation-sign alignment is correct, no diagram or annotations are needed, and editable solution prose/math inherits the supplied blue styling. Examples 0–13 and all mappings are preserved. Baseline existing examples remain empty. Practice and quiz mathematics were neither changed nor re-audited; no files were written.

examples.derivation: Source Q10(b) supports single-category selection. C(11,3)=165 and C(6,3)=20; 20/165=4/33.
Source Q12(c) supports fixed-composition counting. C(5,2)C(7,2)=10×21=210; C(12,4)=495; probability=14/33.
Combinations Q11(f) and Probability Q13(e) support disjoint composition cases. Counts are 350, 175 and 21, totalling 546; 546/C(12,5)=546/792=91/132.
Source Q13(d) supports the no-target complement. C(8,3)=56 and C(12,3)=220; 1−56/220=41/55.
Source Q19(b) and Q20(b) support pair grouping and its complement. Together: 6!×2!/7!=2/7; apart: 1−2/7=5/7.
Source Q6(a,b) supports subject blocks. Favourable arrangements=3!×2!×3!×4!=1728; total=9!=362880; probability=1/210.
Source Q16(a) supports two alternating patterns. Favourable arrangements=2×5!×5!=28800; dividing by 10!=3628800 gives 1/126.
Interpret (d) supports circular grouping. Three friends form one of six units; favourable arrangements=5!×3!=720, total=7!=5040; probability=1/7.

Source Q26(b) supports fixing one person and counting opposite seats. One of Eli's nine remaining seats is opposite Noor, giving 1/9. The planar diagram has ten equally spaced seats and places Noor and Eli diametrically opposite; its annotations occur only in the solution.
Source Q30(b) supports filling the restricted units position first. Total=6P3=120; favourable=3×5P2=60; probability=1/2.

Source Q30(d) supports digit-sum classification followed by arrangement. Independently enumerating the ten three-digit subsets gives exactly {2,3,4}, {2,4,6}, {3,4,5} and {4,5,6} with sums divisible by three. Probability=4×3!/5P3=24/60=2/5.
Source Q21(c) supports subtracting short-gap cases. Zero, one and two intervening letters give 1440, 1200 and 960 arrangements respectively. Their sum is 3600; 1−3600/5040=2/7.

Source Q14(g) supports multiplying one-card selections from distinct categories; selecting the three suits uses the booklet's combination method. Favourable hands=C(4,3)×13³=8788; total=C(52,3)=22100; probability=169/425.
Source Q34(g) supports choosing a suit then its cards. Favourable hands=4×C(13,6)=6864; total=C(52,6)=20358520. Dividing numerator and denominator by 104 gives 66/195755 in lowest terms.

Source Q34(e) supports distinct triple and pair ranks. Favourable hands=9×C(4,3)×8×C(4,2)=1728; total=C(36,5)=376992. Their greatest common divisor is 288, giving 6/1309. The rank roles are distinct, so no division by two applies.
